claims.text: High-temperature stability of multi-element nanoparticles is governed by suppression of surface diffusion.
Maintaining a high-entropy, near-equiatomic atomic mixture suppresses surface diffusion.
A thin passivating dopant layer reduces surface atomic mobility.
A passivating dopant layer will preserve nanoparticle structural and chemical stability relative to an untreated control.
The initial material is a multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticle system with low noble-metal content.
Tungsten is an example of a low-diffusivity element suitable for forming the proposed surface shell.
The proposed intervention is deposition of a thin, controlled dopant shell on as-synthesized nanoparticles.
The relevant catalytic operating range is 773–1173 K.
The relevant thermoelectric operating range is 473–1923 K.
Reducing surface atomic mobility and diffusion helps retain a uniform, high-entropy, near-equiatomic state.
Reducing surface atomic mobility and diffusion prevents elemental segregation.
Elevated temperatures enhance surface diffusion in multi-element nanoparticles.
Enhanced surface diffusion can trigger elemental segregation or phase separation in multi-element nanoparticles.
Impeding surface-atom migration preserves the system's configurational entropy.
Preserving configurational entropy maintains the structural and chemical stability required for catalytic and thermoelectric performance.
Dopant-coated nanoparticles will exhibit less degradation of catalytic conversion efficiency or thermoelectric performance over time than undoped nanoparticles.
Dopant-coated nanoparticles will undergo less morphological change than undoped nanoparticles.
The magnitude of diffusion suppression may depend on dopant identity and deposition quality.
The effect may not be universal across different elemental combinations and service conditions.

Failure to observe a statistically significant reduction in performance degradation, morphological change, or elemental segregation in coated particles relative to undoped controls would falsify the hypothesis.
